articles.body: Greater China Operations The missing middle in Hong Kong’s maritime workforce Splash November 19, 2026 0 1 4 minutes read Hong Kong Cyberport Hong Kong Cyberport The city wants to expand its role in global shipping, but its maritime ambitions face a stubborn recruitment problem. Finding graduates is one thing; attracting and retaining the experienced professionals needed to run an international maritime centre is quite another. Hong Kong has no shortage of ambitions for its maritime industry. It wants to become a centre for green fuel trading, ship finance, digital technology and sophisticated fleet management. But there is one asset that cannot be imported overnight: an experienced marine superintendent who has spent years at sea and knows how to keep an increasingly complex fleet operating safely. The city’s problem is not simply persuading school-leavers to consider a career in shipping. It is attracting and retaining the people 10 or 15 years further along, when hard-won technical knowledge meets commercial judgment and when employers in Singapore, mainland China and industries far beyond shipping are competing for the same individuals. Revealing numbers The Vocational Training Council’s latest maritime manpower survey counts 25,993 employees in 2024, including non-Hong Kong seafarers, with 13,746 in shore-based jobs. It records just 384 vacancies, including 192 ashore, but a 9.1% turnover rate among shore-based staff. A low snapshot vacancy rate does not mean companies can easily find a chief engineer turned superintendent, an experienced claims handler or a specialist surveyor. Richard Hext, chairman of the Hong Kong Shipowners Association, says “talent is one of the sector’s most urgent execution challenges”. Hong Kong needs not just new graduates, he argues, but professionals who can move from seagoing and technical roles into commercial and leadership positions. Earlier VTC research identified a hollowed-out middle in high-value maritime services, with senior staff nearing retirement and junior employees still acquiring experience. It also identified a shortage of people with seagoing qualifications for jobs such as port captain, technical superintendent and ship surveyor. Even the Marine Department has struggled to fill its specialist positions. At classification society RINA, the shortage is practical rather than theoretical. Brian Yam, its commercial director for Hong Kong and Taiwan, says one particular difficulty is hiring experienced ship surveyors locally. Local pathways into naval architecture and marine engineering are limited, and relatively few Hong Kong youngsters spend the years at sea needed to acquire the qualifications and experience employers want. Career ladders There is a fundamental timing problem. A short course can teach a new regulation; it cannot produce the judgment gained from an engine-room failure, a drydocking or years of managing crews and contractors. Shipmanagers are responding by building their own career ladders. Anglo-Eastern chief executive Bjorn Hojgaard says five members of the company’s executive management team started their careers at sea and approximately 75% of its shore managers have been promoted from its seagoing workforce. “Mid-career is the point where many professionals weigh a move into adjacent sectors,” he says. Employers must offer progression, mentoring and competitive rewards before valuable experience walks out of the maritime sector altogether. Quality of life Hong Kong is also competing on quality of life. Housing costs, education, family considerations and alternative careers in finance, technology and family offices affect whether a specialist accepts a posting or stays for the long term. Tax concessions for maritime businesses are of limited use if they create additional corporate structures without bringing experienced decision-makers and their families to the city. Vikrant Gusain, chief executive of Dockendale Group, makes a revealing point about the labour market. At mid-career, people make decisions based on “career optionality — having 10 potential employers rather than two”. An attractive maritime centre therefore needs competing companies, not merely a few very large ones. Recruitment becomes easier when changing jobs does not also mean changing countries. Insurance faces much the same challenge. Deborah Yu, regional director for Asia at London P&I, says: “Mid-career professionals are mobile and have attractive opportunities in many other regional hubs.” Underwriters, claims handlers and specialist surveyors need both competitive remuneration and credible prospects of advancement. The technical requirements are changing, too. Methanol and ammonia, cyber security, emissions verification, remote monitoring and AI are creating new jobs while changing established ones. Ioannis Stefanou, managing director of shipmanagement at Wallem Group, says the competition for skilled professionals extends far beyond shipping. The industry needs to show younger recruits that maritime careers are global, technologically advanced and connected to decarbonisation rather than simply selling a lifetime of paperwork and port calls. Progress There are signs of action. The Hong Kong Shipowners Association launched its academy earlier this month, building on a 16-organisation Maritime Talent Cultivation Alliance established last year. The academy is intended to upgrade members’ knowledge and skills, not simply introduce schoolchildren to the industry. The government’s September policy address also proposed a maritime academy and an institution-enterprise training model with clearer cross-disciplinary career pathways. Training already has tangible public backing. Hong Kong pays eligible deck and engineer cadets HK$10,000 a month during qualifying sea service, and its maritime training fund supports further professional courses and examinations. In April, the government and industry partners organised a train-the-trainer programme on green marine fuels, recognising that new bunkering infrastructure is of little value without people who know how to use it safely. Hext says maritime careers must become “more visible, portable and future-facing”. Structured internships, recognised sea-to-shore qualifications and mid-career transfers could help turn isolated training programmes into genuine progression routes. The next test is not how many academies open or how many students attend a career fair. It is how many surveyors, fleet managers, brokers, claims specialists and marine engineers actually take posts in Hong Kong, and how many remain five years later. The city can fund a ship, register it and insure it. Keeping the know-how needed to operate all three businesses may be the more demanding investment. U.S. Central Command/Handout via REUTERS LONDON, Nov 18 (Reuters) – The US military will treat ships that receive cargo at sea from vessels loaded in Iran as attempting to evade its blockade of Iranian ports and could take action against them, according to an advisory issued by US Central Command (CENTCOM) on Wednesday. The US naval blockade on Iran-related oil exports was first imposed on April 13 and lifted in June after Washington reached a draft understanding with Tehran. It was reimposed on July 14 after the agreement collapsed. “Any ship that receives cargo via a ship-to-ship transfer with a vessel subject to the blockade and carrying cargo loaded at an Iranian port or coastline may be considered to be evading the blockade, even if it has not entered Iranian ports or the Iranian coastline,” CENTCOM said in an update. “Such ships may be stopped, boarded, diverted, captured, or directed to proceed to the Iranian port where the cargo originated.” @5thForces / NAVCENT #NCAGS BLOCKADE OF IRANIAN PORTS Update as of 18 Nov 2026 — The blockade will not impede neutral transit passage through the Strait of Hormuz to or from non-Iranian destinations. Iran has managed to export some liquefied petroleum gas and jet fuel since July, despite the US naval blockade, according to shipping intelligence and security sources who spoke to Reuters in October. Iran’s crude exports, however, have remained near a standstill for months, shipping sources say. (Reporting by Jonathan Saul. Editing by Mark Potter) (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026. articles.title: Ukrainian Drone Attacks Halve Russian Oil Refining in November
articles.summary: Ukrainian drone attacks have slashed Russian oil refineries' combined crude processing volumes by 45% since late October, according to estimates from two industry sources, as Kyiv ramps up strikes on energy infrastructure.Russia is already facing…
articles.body: Ukrainian Drone Attacks Halve Russian Oil Refining in November Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 18, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Sunshine Seeds Ukrainian drone attacks have slashed Russian oil refineries' combined crude processing volumes by 45% since late October, according to estimates from two industry sources, as Kyiv ramps up strikes on energy infrastructure. Russia is already facing domestic fuel shortages in some regions and restricted ex port capacity due to crippling Ukrainian strikes on port s. Reduced refining could also tighten global fuel markets and hamper Russia's ability to deliver on a deal to ex port diesel to the United States. The attacks now have disrupted or halted operations at 15 of Russia's 35 major refineries, the two people said, up from 9 in the middle of last week. Russia's energy ministry did not respond to a Reuters request for comment. MOSCOW AND KYIV RAMPING UP STRIKES ON ENERGY TARGETS US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on October 11. Though neither Moscow nor Kyiv acknowledged agreeing to it and attacks continued, Ukrainian strikes did ease for roughly two weeks. The war has since intensified, however, with Ukrainian drone attacks increasing in scale and frequency as Russia ramps up its own drone and missile strikes. Ukraine hit a strategically im port ant bridge and targeted oil refineries this week in what Russian ‌defence ministry data showed on Monday was the biggest overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of the war in 2022. Following near-daily drone strikes over the last 20 days, crude processing volumes at Russian refineries have fallen to around 400,000 metric tons per day, or around 3 million barrels per day, from over 700,000 metric tons per day at the end of October, the estimates showed. The combined nominal capacity of Russian refineries affected by the attacks since late October stands at around 500,000 tons per day, equivalent to approximately 54% of the country's total primary refining capacity of an estimated 930,000 tons per day. However, the sources said that, given the gradual reduction in operating capacity, average crude processing volumes in November remain above 500,000 tons per day, about 5% to 10% below September and October levels. Major Russian refineries affected by the attacks include plants in Ryazan, Yaroslavl, Kirishi and the Volga region, the people said. (Reuters)

articles.body: Hong Kong Maritime Week joins hands across the sea to address pressing issues for the industry in International Shipping News 18/11/2026 The 10th anniversary edition of Hong Kong Maritime Week (HKMW) (November 15 – 21) is expecting more than 18,000 policymakers, industry leaders, business decision-makers and experts from around the world to explore the latest development opportunities and challenges for the global maritime industry. HKMW comprises over 60 events, including high-level conferences and seminars, organised by more than 80 local, Chinese Mainland and overseas maritime organisations. Priority topics include green transition, high value-added maritime services, smart port and international co-operation. Speaking at the Grand Opening Ceremony (November 16), John Lee, Chief Executive of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR), said that the international maritime industry is undergoing an unprecedented period of transformation. “This year’s theme, ‘Trusted Resilience Powering Global Maritime Trade’, reflects the pivotal juncture we find ourselves at today. International shipowners and shipping enterprises are navigating daunting headwinds, powered by complex geopolitical shifts, supply chain fragmentation and heightened market volatility. Such testing waters demand steady hands and decisive leadership,” Mr Lee said. “In times of complexity, we look for certainty. Under the enduring principle of ‘one country, two systems’, Hong Kong stands proudly as the international shipping community’s ‘safe harbour’.” Mr Lee also announced the formation of the Task Group on the Development of the Green Maritime Fuel Trading Platform. This, he said, would bring together leading industry experts to advise on strategic direction, infrastructure set-up and price discovery mechanism. During the Grand Opening Ceremony, a series of important deliverables were announced, underscoring Hong Kong’s crucial dual role as a “super connector” and “super value-adder” linking Chinese Mainland with the rest of the world. The deliverables include: Signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Hainan Yangpu Port to establish a partner port relationship for strengthening co-operation in the port and maritime sectors between Hainan and Hong Kong; Signing an MOU with Zhanjiang, Guangdong, to jointly establish Hong Kong’s first Green Energy Corridor; Signing an MOU with the Port of Piraeus in Greece to jointly establish Hong Kong’s first Green Shipping Corridor and a partner port relationship; and Officially issuing the first protection and indemnity insurance policy of the Hong Kong Shipowners Mutual Assurance Association. HKSAR’s Secretary for Transport and Logistics, Mable Chan, said these achievements fully leverage Hong Kong’s unique advantages of connecting the Chinese Mainland and the world, yielding fruitful results. “Our ecosystem thrives on the rule of law under a trusted common law system, a simple and competitive tax regime, and a world-class cluster of high value-added maritime services supported by top-tier bilingual talent. Hong Kong is the vital ‘super connector’ and ‘super value-adder’ between the Chinese Mainland and global markets,” Ms Chan said. Addressing the Hong Kong Global Maritime Trade Summit (November 16), HKSAR’s Financial Secretary, Paul Chan, identified three trends for the maritime industry, namely, regionalisation of trade; green transition; and artificial intelligence (AI). “On technology and AI, Hong Kong is tackling the issue at its core constraint: data. More than 10,000 enterprises have registered with the Port Community System (PCS) since its rollout in January. Some have begun to secure trade finance on the strength of the PCS’s trusted cargo-flow data,” Mr Chan said. “Under Project CargoX, led by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, 21 banks are testing a faster way to verify trade transactions. Instead of relying on paper documents, they use data shared on a common digital platform, with the data owner’s consent.” During the two-day (November 16 – 17) Asian Logistics, Maritime and Aviation Conference, a flagship event of HKMW, various important achievements were announced in relation to maritime and logistics that materialise green transformation and the connection of logistics networks. These included the signing of three MOUs and the launch of a co-operation initiative, involving the promotion of the development of local sustainable aviation fuel blending facilities, fostering collaboration on green maritime fuels and related certification standards, expanding Hong Kong’s partner port network and establishing a Vietnam-Guangxi-Hong Kong land-air super logistics corridor. The Baltic and International Maritime Council (BIMCO), the world’s largest direct-membership organisation for shipping, is participating in HKMW for the first time. In partnership with the International Organization for Mediation, BIMCO staged a dedicated seminar (November 18) addressing contractual developments in the era of green energy transition and maritime decarbonisation. articles.summary: South Korea’s Lotte Fine Chemical (LFC) and Norwegian shipping company Höegh Autoliners plan to expand green ammonia bunkering operations across South Korean ports. The companies have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to develop green ammonia supply and bunkering infrastructure in South Korea. LFC already...
articles.body: Lotte Fine Chemical and Höegh eye green ammonia bunkering network in South Korea in International Shipping News 18/11/2026 South Korea’s Lotte Fine Chemical (LFC) and Norwegian shipping company Höegh Autoliners plan to expand green ammonia bunkering operations across South Korean ports. The companies have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to develop green ammonia supply and bunkering infrastructure in South Korea. LFC already conducts ammonia bunkering operations at its terminal in Ulsan port. It recently supplied an unspecified quantity of green ammonia to Singapore-based Eastern Pacific Shipping’s first very large ammonia carrier (VLAC). The fuel was produced at Envision Energy’s green ammonia plant in Chifeng, Inner Mongolia, China. The partnership aims to extend these bunkering operations to other South Korean ports, with potential expansion into international markets, LFC said. Höegh Autoliners currently has four ammonia-capable pure car and truck carriers (PCTCs) scheduled for delivery by 2027, according to its website. The company has also ordered six LNG-capable vessels, some of which carry DNV’s ammonia-ready notation. But the shipping firm has not disclosed the extent of their readiness to operate on ammonia. articles.body: ALNG Report Third Quarter Net Loss in International Shipping News 18/11/2026 HIGHLIGHTS •ALNG reports a net loss of USD 5.9 million in the third quarter of 2026, compared to a net loss of 6.4 million in the previous quarter, and a loss per share of USD 0.03. •Net freight income of USD 7.1 million in third quarter of 2026, compared to USD 5.9 million in second quarter of 2026. •EBITDA in third quarter of 2026 ended at USD 0.1 million, down from USD 0.6 million in second quarter of 2026. •Vessel utilization was 73% for third quarter of 2026, compared to 66% for second quarter of 2026. •Net TCE came in at USD 38,400 for third quarter, compared to USD 32,600 the previous quarter. •In October the Company entered into period contracts for both vessels with final period dependent on certain conditions. The contracts are with an international oil major for worldwide trading Jens-Julius Nygaard, Interim Chief Executive Officer, commented: “In third quarter the LNG shipping segment experienced in a decreasing number of cargoes compared with too many available vessels. This led to a continuous drop in spot market rates to levels well below opex at the end of the quarter. This negatively impacted ALNG’s overall earnings and utilization of the fleet in the third quarter, despite having WilPride on TC for most of the quarter. However, in October we managed to secure a TC for both WilPride and WilForce which will provide increased utilization and reduce the substantial cost of being idle with the current high gas prices. The focus for the Company is still on opportunities in both segments as we enter the winter season with very low gas storage in Europe and a volatile gas price.” FINANCIAL REVIEW Income statement third quarter 2026 WilPride ended her six-month charter contract early September 2026 and entered the spot market while WilForce continued to trade in a weak spot market with idle periods throughout third quarter of 2026. The combined TCE ended at USD 38,400 per day on average, up from USD 32,600 in the previous quarter. Freight income for the quarter ended at USD 10.1 million compared to USD 7.3 million in second quarter of 2026. Voyage related expenses were USD 3.0 million, up from USD 1.4 million in second quarter of 2026 as elevated gas prices lead to high cost of fuel. Net freight income for the quarter ended at USD 7.1 million compared to USD 5.9 million in second quarter of 2026. Operating expenses came in at USD 4.1 million in third quarter of 2026 compared to USD 3.8 million in previous quarter and administration expenses were USD 2.9 million in third quarter of 2026. EBITDA for the quarter ended at USD 0.1 million, down from USD 0.6 million in second quarter of 2026. Depreciation charges for the quarter were USD 3.8 million, same as the previous quarter. Net financial expenses were USD 2.2 million in third quarter of 2026, down from USD 3.2 million in second quarter of 2026 as the company paid and expensed costs related to the amendment of its financing agreements in the previous quarter. Running interest expense on the vessels’ financing in third quarter of 2026 amounted to USD 2.7 million, down from USD 2.8 million for the previous quarter. Running interest expenses will fluctuate with the development of SOFR interest rates. Loss and loss per share for the quarter ended at USD 5.9 million and USD 0.03, respectively, compared to a loss of USD 6.4 million and a loss per share of USD 0.03 in second quarter of 2026. Liquidity and financial position Cash and cash equivalents decreased from USD 33.3 million at the end of second quarter of 2026 to USD 29.8 million at the end of third quarter 2026. Cash flow from operations was negative USD 0.8 million compared to USD 1.3 million in second quarter of 2026. There were no investments in vessels or other assets during the quarter. Interest-bearing debt net of capitalized and amortized transaction costs was unchanged throughout the quarter at USD 168.9 million, in accordance with the announced amendment of the lease agreements with CDBL. The current portion of the interest-bearing debt constituted USD 0.1 million only as there are no scheduled amortization of the leases for the 12 months following September 30, 2026, according to the amended terms. Ordinary repayment of the leases resumes in first quarter of 2028, and the deferred amount will be paid during 2029 and 2030. Starting in June 2026 the Group has rolling repurchase options of the vessels and repurchase obligations at maturity of the facility. As of September 30, 2026, total book value of WilForce and WilPride was USD 275.3 million following depreciation of USD 3.8 million and zero capitalization of any investments in the vessels during the quarter. Book equity on September 30, 2026, was USD 135.0 million and total assets were USD 312.0 million, resulting in an equity ratio of 43.3% at quarter-end, somewhat lower than 44.4% at the end of second quarter. MARKET AND CHARTERING UPDATE Third quarter was a quarter of two halves. July opened firm: renewed hostilities around the Strait of Hormuz kept the risk premium intact, portfolio players held tonnage internally and Atlantic availability stayed tight. TFDE spot rates averaged approximately USD 60,000 per day West of Suez and USD 50,000 per day East of Suez in July, with modern two-stroke tonnage briefly exceeding USD 100,000 per day in the Atlantic. From late July the floor fell away. The European gas reference price TTF overtook Asian reference price JKM as European buyers competed for cargoes to rebuild record-low storage, which closed the inter-basin arbitrage, redirected US cargoes into short intra-Atlantic voyages and cut tonne-mile demand just as prompt tonnage was building in both basins. The Atlantic two-stroke benchmark fell from around USD 96,000 per day at the end of July to USD 13,000 per day by the end of August, and TFDE tonnage was fixing at or below USD 10,000 per day – well below operating cost – through August and September. For the quarter, West of Suez TFDE spot averaged USD 28,000 per day (USD 9,500 per day in September), down from approximately USD 62,000 per day in second quarter, while East of Suez TFDE held somewhat better at USD 33,000 per day on premium Middle East business before converging with the Atlantic in September. The imbalance was driven as much by ships as by cargoes. Prompt availability almost doubled, 18 newbuilds were delivered, and relet tonnage from portfolio players and Qatar Energy’s idle Gulf fleet took over half of the spot market and 70% of multi-month fixtures, consistently undercutting independent owners. Near-term chartering activity fell by a third to around 105 fixtures, 84% of them single voyages, and August–September saw the fewest spot fixtures of any two-month period since early 2024. Period rates softened but held well above spot: one-year two-stroke rates eased from around USD 70,000 per day in July to USD 49,000 per day at quarter-end, one-year TFDE was assessed at USD 30,000 per day, and charterers increasingly favoured index-linked structures over fixed rates. WilPride traded on her six-month charter above USD 70,000 per day until redelivery in first half September, which coincided with the weakest point of the quarter and left her competing for limited spot enquiry alongside WilForce, which traded spot with idle periods throughout the quarter. The combined TCE of USD 38,400 per day, above the TFDE spot averages, reflects the charter cover on WilPride through August. With most charterers’ winter requirements already covered and the market not positioned for a rally comparable to November last year, the Company prioritised utilisation over spot optionality and in October the Company entered into period business on both vessels with final period dependent on certain conditions – removing idle exposure and the substantial cost of idling with gas prices above USD 24 per MMBtu through the winter. Market snapshot for third quarter 2026: Global loadings of 103 million tonnes were up around 5 MT on second quarter as US output ran at record levels (Plaquemines, Corpus Christi Stage 3), but Qatari exports remained at roughly a quarter of pre-war volumes with around half of the Gulf-dedicated fleet idle; Hormuz LNG transits nevertheless rose to 45 in September, the most since the war began. European imports fell 16% quarter-on-quarter to 22 MT while Japan, Korea, Taiwan and China took 56 MT (+11%); EU storage ended September at 71%, the lowest for the date since 2011. TTF and JKM both closed the quarter above USD 24 per MMBtu with the Asia–Europe spread close to zero. The conventional fleet stood at 782 vessels at quarter-end after 18 deliveries; 13 vessels were ordered and none sold for scrap in the quarter. The orderbook of 285 vessels (36% of the fleet) includes 31 deliveries due in fourth quarter and 93 in 2027. The S&P market remained active with 21 transactions year-to-date, with demand for older steam tonnage for Hormuz trading supporting second-hand values. ORGANISATION The principal activity of ALNG ASA and its subsidiaries is to invest and operate in LNG vessels and trade in the LNG commodity market. Following the Capital rise in First half of 2026 the Company has continued to build up the LNG Trading platform. The intention for ALNG Trading is to initially develop structured and low risk trading deals. Commercial management of the fleet is performed from the Group’s offices in Oslo and London and technical management is contracted from affiliated and external companies. As per end of third quarter the Group had nine direct employees onshore. ALNG also purchases certain administrative services from the Awilhelmsen Group, see note 5 for further details. VESSEL STATUS In October the Company entered into period business with an international oil major for both vessels with final period dependent on certain conditions. The terms of the TCs have been agreed at favourable levels that reflect market rates for the type of voyages permitted. The total financial impact of the TCs over their duration is uncertain at this time. Realised income, will be provided in ALNG’s fourth quarter report. The Company continues to focus on maximizing revenues from the vessels until long-term employment is available. OUTLOOK The third quarter continued where the second quarter ended and continued its high volatility dominated by the war in the Middle East. The effective reduction in LNG production in the area and also transport through the Strait of Hormuz has shown to be a negative factor for the LNG Shipping market with increased excess of available tonnage in both the Atlantic and Pacific basins. The spot market is weak while we are entering the winter market, and the Company expect this to continue through the prolonged Iran-US conflict and its impact on global LNG trade. The outcome of the conflict and timing of the end to the hostilities are uncertain, making it difficult to forecast reopening of LNG production in the area and the future impact on tonne-miles. The Trading initiative is progressing slower than anticipated partly due to the rapid increase in gas prices globally. In the meantime, the Company continues the complex work to establish the ground for our first LNG Trade. Full Report Source: ALNG 2026-11-18 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: The Mission to Seafarers announces winners of 2026 Seafarers Awards in International Shipping News 18/11/2026 The Mission to Seafarers (MtS), a leading international seafarer welfare charity, is delighted to announce the winners of its 9th International Seafarers Awards, following another successful ceremony held on Friday, 13 November at the Fairmont Hotel, Singapore. The evening celebrated the hard work, sacrifices, and talents of those who tirelessly support one of the world’s most vital workforces. Guy Platten OBE, MtS’s new Chair, opened proceedings at his first Seafarers Awards. The awards brought together longstanding supporters and partners to recognise the individuals and organisations making a real difference to the lives and wellbeing of seafarers. The evening also served as a continuation of The Mission to Seafarers Singapore’s (MtSS) Centenary celebrations and saw the launch of the Centenary Appeal, which aims to help strengthen and develop the work of MtSS in the years ahead. The room, which welcomed over 400 guests, was filled with anticipation as the night’s winners were announced. Over 150 nominations were submitted, more than double the number for 2025, highlighting the significance and popularity of the awards. MtS would like to thank its Founding Gold Sponsors BHP and Shell, Gold Sponsor Pacific International Lines (PIL), Silver Sponsors Fleet Management Limited, NorthStandard, West P&I, SOS, SMOU and Arrow, as well as Videography Sponsor DNV, Glass Awards Sponsor ATPI and Drinks Reception Sponsor HFW, for their continued support of this important celebration. All winners receiving their awards Congratulations to the winners of the 2026 Seafarers Awards: Seafarer Award – The seafarer who has made a significant contribution to welfare at sea. • Winner: Captain Lulian Ene, Anglo-Eastern Ship Management (Hellas) Shore-based Award – The shore-based person who has made a significant contribution to seafarers’ welfare. • Winner: Purnima Lama, Eastern Pacific Shipping • Highly Commended: Vitalii Chaika, ASP Crew Management Cadet Award – The cadet or trainee who has made a significant contribution to seafarers’ welfare at sea or ashore. • Winner: Nino Candol, Eastern Pacific Shipping • Highly Commended: Wayne Jacel P. Bugtong, IMMAJ, Maranaw Luzon Shipping Company Innovation Award – The company that has embraced a new programme, project, or training which has enhanced seafarers’ welfare. • Winner: Marlow Navigation • Highly Commended: Eastern Pacific Shipping, Sous Chef Programme • Highly Commended: Agwa Rescue Award – The captain or crew who has coordinated a successful rescue operation to save lives at sea. • Winner: Captain Vishal Naik and the crew of the Golden Beijing, Bernhard Schulte Ship Management • Highly Commended: Captain Keegan Denis Patrao and the crew of the Pacific Crystal, Eastern Pacific Shipping Secretary General Award – The person or company who has shown sustained efforts to improve seafarers’ welfare at sea or ashore. • Winner: Captain Abhishek Chawla, Pacific International Lines (PIL) • Highly Commended: Eastern Pacific Shipping • Highly Commended: Swire Shipping’s fleet team, led by Stuart Jones and Jesmark Ramos Jan Webber, Director of Development at The Mission to Seafarers, said: “The 2026 Seafarers Awards recognise people and organisations who go well beyond what is asked of them to look after seafarers. From a rescue at sea to a cadet already making a difference to the crew around them, this year’s winners show that seafarer welfare is built through individual action, at every rank, at sea and ashore. We warmly congratulate all our winners and highly commended entrants, and thank every nominee. Our gratitude also extends to our sponsors and partners, whose generous support makes this evening, and our work in ports around the world, possible.” The Lucky Draw was another highlight of the evening, featuring coveted prizes such as an SGD 1,000 travel voucher courtesy of ATPI, two cases of wine from Vergelegen Estate courtesy of Anglo American, tickets to Albatross Island courtesy of Royal Albatross, a one-night stay for two at the Singapore Polo Club, and more. The Lucky Draw and Silent Auction together raised over SGD 15,000. These prizes reflected the strong support and appreciation that the industry and partners have for MtS and for the seafarers who keep our global economy moving. MtS is equally thankful to all who donated the eight sought-after Lucky Draw prizes. Some of the award winners, highly commended, Gold Sponsors pose for a photo with The Mission to Seafarer’s Secretary General, Peter Rouch and Director of Development, Jan Webber. Teng Huar Lee, Vice President, Shipping and Maritime APME Shell, said: “For 100 years, The Mission to Seafarers Singapore has stood alongside seafarers. Shell is proud to continue our support and partnership to that journey, working with the maritime community to turn care into action and support the wellbeing of the people behind every voyage.” Emma Roberts, Vice President Maritime and Supply Chain Excellence, BHP, said: “Congratulations to The Mission to Seafarers and this year’s winners of its 9th International Seafarers Awards. For 170 years, The Mission to Seafarers has played an important role supporting the welfare of seafarers and recognising their contribution to global trade. Seafarers spend extended periods at sea away from their families to keep global trade moving. Ensuring they are recognised and supported is incredibly important for the industry and why we are proud to support this initiative.” Lars Kastrup, CEO, Pacific International Lines, said: “Behind every vessel and every voyage are seafarers whose dedication keeps global trade moving. We are proud to stand with The Mission to Seafarers in recognising their contributions and supporting their wellbeing. I am especially encouraged by the young maritime talent recognised this evening, and I hope they will continue to build rewarding and fulfilling careers at sea.” Join The Mission to Seafarers next year to celebrate further outstanding contributions to seafarers’ welfare. For sponsorship or general enquiries about the next Seafarers Awards in 2027, please email Jan Webber ( [email protected] ). articles.body: All 19 crew members rescued after gas carrier ‘struck’ in Black Sea off Bulgaria in International Shipping News 18/11/2026 It marks the latest in a string of similar incidents in the Black Sea believed to be linked to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. All 19 crew members were rescued after a gas carrier was “struck” in the Black Sea off Bulgaria on Tuesday, authorities and the ship’s management company said. Stealth Maritime, the Greek management company, confirmed in a statement that the Gas Husky had been “struck” early on Tuesday morning as it was sailing within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. It did not clarify what had hit the Liberian-flagged carrier. “The vessel was carrying a cargo of LPG loaded in Alexandria, Egypt, and was heading to Midia, Romania, for discharge,” it said, adding that the ship’s condition was currently unknown. According to Bulgaria’s ministry of transport, the vessel was carrying 3,400 tonnes of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) before it disappeared from radar shortly after midnight. It then sent a distress signal at around 8:02 am, around 50 nautical miles east of Byala. “Upon receiving the distress signal, assistance was requested from the air force to conduct an aerial survey of the area. During the survey, an overturned vessel was identified, believed to be the Gas Husky vessel,” the ministry said in a statement. “About 300 metres away, a life raft was spotted, from which a distress flare was launched.” The crew were rescued from the life raft and flown by helicopter to the Chaika air base in Varna, it added. It marks the latest in a string of similar incidents in the Black Sea believed to be linked to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. On Monday, 12 people were rescued after the Somali-flagged Betul 8 cargo ship capsized off the coast of Bulgaria following a suspected drone strike. The Betul 8 had been travelling from Tulcea in Romania to Egypt and was carrying almost 3,000 tonnes of bulk wheat, authorities said. The European Union has pledged €50 million for a Black Sea Maritime Security Hub hosted by Bulgaria and Romania to help combat security threats in the region. The bloc has also committed a further €10 million in funds to help bolster Bulgaria’s search and rescue operations. Source: Euronews 2026-11-18 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Ravenna: Nova Marine Carriers acquires a 25% stake in Terminal Nord S.p.A. in Port News 18/11/2026 Sider Navi S.r.l., the Italian sub-holding company of the international shipping group Nova Marine Carriers, based in Lugano, has acquired a 25% stake in Terminal Nord S.p.A., a port terminal operator belonging to the Sapir Group at the Port of Ravenna. The transaction is the result of a strategy shared by both Sapir S.p.A. and Nova Marine, aimed at providing customers with increasingly integrated logistics solutions combining maritime transport and port terminal operations. Nova Marine’s entry into Terminal Nord’s shareholding structure is therefore based on a shared industrial vision, designed to generate new operational synergies and support the growth and competitiveness of the Port of Ravenna in the short and medium term. As part of the partnership, Terminal Nord S.p.A. will continue to rely on the strong infrastructure base and the operational, administrative and institutional management provided by Sapir S.p.A., the leading business group operating in the Port of Ravenna. At the same time, Nova Marine will support the majority shareholder by contributing its international shipping expertise and taking responsibility for coordinating the terminal’s commercial development. Vincenzo Romeo, CEO of Nova Marine Carriers “We are delighted to welcome the Nova Marine Group as a shareholder in Terminal Nord,” says Riccardo Sabadini, Chairman of Terminal Nord S.p.A. and Sapir S.p.A. “This transaction brings together our Group’s well-established operational and infrastructural capabilities with the in-depth knowledge of international maritime markets offered by a leading operator such as Nova Marine. This industrial partnership is focused on the future of the Port of Ravenna and is designed to further strengthen the terminal’s attractiveness, create new development opportunities and respond even more effectively to the needs of customers and the wider logistics supply chain.” “Joining Terminal Nord represents a key strategic milestone in the growth and consolidation of the Nova Marine Carriers Group,” comments Vincenzo Romeo, CEO of Nova Marine Carriers. “We are highly motivated by the opportunities arising from this further collaboration with a partner such as Sapir S.p.A. We will make our global network, fleet and experience in the transportation of dry bulk and other cargo categories available to further enhance the potential of a terminal that is strategically important for the Adriatic region”. November 18, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Grispb Most Gulf stocks closed lower on Wednesday following Iran's strike on Kuwait, the first since September, targeting US drone and missile sites and raising fears of further escalation after Washington hit Qeshm Island. Iran's army said it targeted US installations at Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem base, the first Iranian attack on the oil-rich country since September, while Bahrain said it intercepted Iranian aerial attacks for the third time this week. Saudi Arabia's benchmark index dropped 0.5%, after Saudi National Bank, the country's biggest lender by assets, fell 1.1%. Dubai's main index lost 0.2%, with toll operator Salik Co retreating 0.9%. Kuwait's premier index slipped 0.1%. Elsewhere, the Qatari index finished flat, with Qatar Islamic Bank losing 0.6%. articles.title: More U.S. LNG Cargoes Divert to Europe in Relief for Tight Market
articles.summary: More liquefied natural gas vessels have diverted toward Europe in recent days, bolstering supplies in a tight market and pressuring prices.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network File Photo: Igor Grochev / Shutterstock (Bloomberg) — More liquefied natural gas vessels have diverted toward Europe in recent days, bolstering supplies in a tight market and pressuring prices. At least two tankers carrying US LNG have rerouted recently away from Egypt in the Mediterranean Sea, according to ship-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg and intelligence firm Kpler. That’s in addition to two ships laden with US fuel that turned sharply north toward Europe, diverting away from Asia, since last week. The diversions come amid weaker demand from some major buyers in Asia — where LNG prices have fetched a discount to Europe — and other regions, although global supplies remain tight because of continued disruptions in the Middle East. The LNG flows to Europe have helped curb prices there, after benchmark gas futures hit an almost four-year high last month. Read More: European Gas Slips as Steady Supply Tempers Mideast Worries Despite persistent shipping risks in the Strait of Hormuz, there has been an uptick in flows from LNG giant Qatar, and less competition between Asia and Europe for cargoes, Kpler principal gas and LNG analyst Ronald Pinto said. For Egypt, the recent price rallies made spot LNG purchases more expensive, and there have also been some capacity expansions scheduled to increase gas flows from Israel to Egypt, he said. Egypt’s cabinet earlier this month approved a rationing plan for power consumption that state bodies will implement during the current financial year to cope with the spillover effects of the Iran war. Egypt had to curb some electricity usage this year as it grappled with high fuel costs due to the conflict. The Al Qassar tanker, carrying US LNG, turned west away from Egypt earlier this week after reaching the country’s Port Said, according to ship-tracking data. Kpler estimates it’s now heading toward Europe. The Amaryllis Knutsen vessel, also loaded with US fuel, made a sharp U-turn on Tuesday near Egypt. Separately, there’s been a diversion from Egypt toward Asia recently, based on Kpler and data on Bloomberg, with the Greenergy Wind tanker turning south in the mid-Atlantic on Tuesday. It’s signaling the Cape of Good Hope, a usual route toward Asia. A sustained fall in LNG spot prices could prompt buyers in South and Southeast Asia to purchase more cargoes, especially as big importers remain on the sidelines, according to traders. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: The US military will treat ships that receive cargo at sea from vessels loaded in Iran as attempting to evade its blockade of Iranian ports and could take action against them, according to an advisory issued by US Central Command (CENTCOM) on…
articles.body: US Cracks Down on Iran Oil Blockade, Threatening Action Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 18, 2026 © Adobe Stock/alones The US military will treat ships that receive cargo at sea from vessels loaded in Iran as attempting to evade its blockade of Iranian ports and could take action against them, according to an advisory issued by US Central Command (CENTCOM) on Wednesday. The US naval blockade on Iran-related oil exports was first imposed on April 13 and lifted in June after Washington reached a draft understanding with Tehran. It was reimposed on July 14 after the agreement collapsed. "Any ship that receives cargo via a ship-to-ship transfer with a vessel subject to the blockade and carrying cargo loaded at an Iranian port or coastline may be considered to be evading the blockade, even if it has not entered Iranian ports or the Iranian coastline," CENTCOM said in an update. "Such ships may be stopped, boarded, diverted, captured, or directed to proceed to the Iranian port where the cargo originated." Ships that fail to comply immediately with lawful orders from blockade or boarding forces could face enforcement action, "including the use of force consistent with applicable law", the advisory added. Iran has managed to export some liquefied petroleum gas and jet fuel since July, despite the US naval blockade, according to shipping intelligence and security sources who spoke to Reuters in October. Iran's crude exports, however, have remained near a standstill for months, shipping sources say. (Reuters)

(Source: NTSB/U.S. Coast Guard) A Houston ship pilot has been indicted on a federal seaman’s manslaughter charge over a deadly 2024 collision in the Houston Ship Channel, in what federal officials describe as the first prosecution of its kind involving a ship pilot. Darris Ornel Jefferson, 39, is accused of misconduct, negligence and inattention to his duties while piloting the bulk carrier Yangze 7 on July 19, 2024, when it collided with the towing vessel Miss Peggy near Lynchburg, Texas, according to the U.S. Department of Justice . The Miss Peggy capsized and sank with five crewmembers aboard. Four were rescued, while a fifth, identified in court records as 25-year-old deckhand Aquarius Lowman, was later found dead in the wreckage. One surviving crewmember suffered serious injuries and another sustained minor injuries. The indictment follows a National Transportation Safety Board investigation released in August that found the pilot had been distracted by an extended, nonoperational cellphone conversation with another pilot while navigating the busy waterway. Investigators determined that the call lasted 39 minutes and ended just two minutes and 16 seconds before the collision. The distraction contributed to the pilot’s failure to detect the Miss Peggy ahead of the bulk carrier. The NTSB also identified failures elsewhere on the vessels. The Yangze 7 bridge team did not detect the towboat until it was less than a ship’s length ahead, while the Miss Peggy captain failed to detect the bulk carrier approaching from astern. Investigators concluded that the collision resulted from a loss of situational awareness by the pilot, the bulk carrier’s bridge team and the towboat’s captain due to failures to maintain proper lookouts. The investigation also found that the Houston Pilots organization had no policy at the time prohibiting nonoperational use of personal electronic devices by pilots directing vessel movements. The NTSB subsequently recommended that the Coast Guard and American Pilots’ Association establish restrictions on such use. The American Pilots’ Association, responding to the NTSB findings in August, said the pilot’s performance had fallen short of professional standards and pledged to work with regulators to strengthen safeguards against distracted navigation. The collision caused an estimated $3.7 million in damages, salvage expenses and pollution mitigation costs, according to the NTSB. The criminal indictment now places the incident under a federal statute that allows prosecutors to pursue charges against maritime officers and others whose misconduct, negligence or inattention results in a death. If convicted, Jefferson faces up to 10 years in federal prison and a $250,000 fine. Jefferson is scheduled to make his initial appearance before U.S. Magistrate Judge Christina Bryan on November 24. The Coast Guard investigated the case, which is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Jason E. Corley. The allegations have not been proven in court, and Jefferson is presumed innocent unless convicted. ABC Affiliate WGNO via REUTERS The U.S. Coast Guard has established a temporary safety zone on the Mississippi River in New Orleans through December 11 as salvage crews prepare to recover the American Heritage river cruise ship, which capsized after being struck by a tanker last week. The temporary final rule, published Wednesday in the Federal Register, formalizes restrictions first imposed November 13 following the collision between the tanker Atlantic Asphalt and the docked American Cruise Lines vessel near the Crescent City Connection Bridge. The safety zone covers a one-mile stretch of the Lower Mississippi River between mile markers 95.5 and 96.5, extending 500 feet from the left descending bank, or east bank. Vessels and personnel are prohibited from entering the restricted area without authorization from the Captain of the Port of New Orleans. The Coast Guard said the restrictions are necessary because of potential debris in the water and hazards associated with salvage vessels, personnel and heavy equipment. Recovery operations are expected to take several weeks, although the safety zone may be canceled before December 11 if conditions permit. The zone does not amount to a monthlong shutdown of the Mississippi River. According to a November 16 update from the City of New Orleans, the alternate navigation channel remains closed, but limited two-way traffic is permitted through the main span of the Crescent City Connection Bridge. Deep-draft vessels and towing vessels pushing 10 or more barges remain restricted to one-way transit. The November 13 collision caused American Heritage to capsize alongside the pier, triggering a major rescue operation involving federal and local emergency responders and nearby commercial vessels. According to the National Transportation Safety Board, 190 passengers and crew were aboard the riverboat at the time of the accident, with 36 people hospitalized. All personnel aboard both vessels were accounted for. The NTSB is leading the investigation into the collision. A unified command comprising the Coast Guard and American Cruise Lines has been established to oversee lightering and salvage operations. Divers began inspecting the submerged vessel on November 15 to assess hull damage and help develop a recovery plan. Containment boom has also been deployed around the wreck as a precaution. New Orleans officials said Monday that an initial sheen had dissipated and no additional pollution had been observed. The Coast Guard said it will continue monitoring conditions and issue updated navigation restrictions as the salvage operation progresses. articles.summary: A potential strike at the nation’s busiest container port complex is back on the table after contract negotiations between waterfront employers and a union representing about 250 port security workers...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network The shipping ports of Los Angeles (top left) and Long Beach are seen from the window of a commercial aircraft over Long Beach, California, U.S. March 13, 2023. REUTERS/Chris Helgren A potential strike at the nation’s busiest container port complex is back on the table after contract negotiations between waterfront employers and a union representing about 250 port security workers failed to produce a breakthrough. The Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) warned Wednesday that members of International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 could walk off the job as early as 12:01 a.m. Saturday, November 21, when their latest contract extension expires. According to PMA, Tuesday’s negotiations ended with little progress, and the union has indicated it is unwilling to agree to another extension. The two sides are scheduled to meet again Friday, leaving little time to avert a potential disruption. Although Local 26 represents just 2% of the ILWU workforce at the ports, its members provide security at six container terminals responsible for more than half of the cargo moving through the Los Angeles-Long Beach port complex. Those terminals handle approximately 85% of Long Beach’s cargo and 33% of Los Angeles’ cargo, according to PMA. The concern is that a strike by the watchmen could quickly spread beyond the 250 workers directly involved in the dispute. Thousands of longshore workers, marine clerks and foremen covered by separate labor agreements are expected to honor Local 26 picket lines, potentially bringing vessel operations, container movements and truck access to a halt at affected terminals. The dispute comes at a particularly sensitive time for the Southern California supply chain, with the ports handling heavy cargo volumes ahead of the holiday shopping season. A prolonged shutdown could disrupt rail and trucking operations, delay imports and exports, and create congestion extending well beyond the waterfront. Employers Detail Contract Offer PMA said its latest proposal includes a one-time $3,200 bonus for each Local 26 member and wage increases that would raise average annual earnings for full-time watchmen from more than $170,000 to $198,000. The association said the offer would also preserve fully employer-paid healthcare for active workers and retirees, which it values at more than $62,000 annually, while increasing annual pension benefits to as much as $93,200 for the longest-serving workers. PMA accused the union of making little movement on its demands despite more than a year of negotiations, including talks assisted by the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service. The union’s response to the latest employer proposals was not immediately available. Local 26 members are responsible for checking identification and credentials at terminal gates, conducting security patrols and reporting safety concerns. Their previous labor agreement expired in July 2025, with workers continuing under a series of extensions. The dispute is separate from the coastwide labor agreement covering most West Coast dockworkers, which runs through 2028. Economic Stakes PMA pointed to an analysis by maritime economist John Martin estimating that the six affected terminals handled approximately 6.2 million containers in 2025 and supported nearly 4.2 million jobs nationwide through direct and indirect economic activity. The analysis attributed $885 billion in national economic activity to cargo moving through those facilities last year. That figure represents the economic activity associated with the terminals, not an estimate of losses from a potential strike. PMA warned that losses could mount rapidly if vessels are unable to discharge cargo and containers already inside the terminals cannot be moved out. articles.title: FMC Advisory — Documented Export Policies Must be Filed with the FMC by March 1 Each Year
articles.summary: In order to enable the timely and efficient movement of export cargo, ocean common carriers transporting containerized cargo are required to file documented export policies as set forth in 46 CFR 542.1(j), issued as part of the Commission’s final rule…
articles.body: FMC Advisory — Documented Export Policies Must be Filed with the FMC by March 1 Each Year Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 18, 2026 Image courtesy FMC In order to enable the timely and efficient movement of export cargo, ocean common carriers transporting containerized cargo are required to file documented export policies as set forth in 46 CFR 542.1(j), issued as part of the Commission’s final rule, “Definition of Unreasonable Refusal to Deal or Negotiate with Respect to Vessel Space Accommodations Provided by an Ocean Common Carrier” issued in 2024. Common carriers must annually submit their documented export policy on or before March 1 each year. 90 FR 30 (Jan. 2, 2025); see also 46 CFR 542.1(j)(1). Failure to file as set forth below will constitute a violation of a federal regulation. Filing Instructions Unless superseded by subsequent Commission order or filing instructions issued by the Commission: 1. Ocean common carriers must file their documented export policy with the Commission on or before March 1 each calendar year. A documented export policy should cover the period until the next policy is due for submission. Common carriers may file updated versions more frequently as needed. 2. Documents must be submitted in English, and any monetary terms shall be expressed in terms of U.S. currency. 3. Documented export policies must be submitted via email to: [email protected] . 4. Each of the following items must be addressed in a documented export policy. The Commission provides the following guidance on how a carrier can best address each topic: “Pricing strategies” – The common carrier’s criteria for pricing export cargo space in service contracts, tariffs, and spot rates, detailing key cost drivers and their relative importance, including operational costs, vessel capacity utilization, equipment inventory levels, equipment repositioning and trade imbalance, as well as a discussion of how these factors are incorporated into pricing; whether customers are notified within a pre-determined timeframe, and details as to what that timeframe is, before any changes to freight rates, surcharges, or fees are implemented. “Markets served” and “Services offered” – (1) Each geographic/export market in which the common carrier offers service, in reasonable detail. (2) The export services the common carrier makes available within each market, including routes, sailing frequency, service alternatives/substitutes, and conditions for negotiating and accepting export bookings, especially to the extent such conditions differ from conditions applied to import bookings. “Strategies for equipment provision” – How the common carrier determines the availability, allocation, and positioning of equipment in support of exports, including empty containers; how equipment inventory is monitored and allocated across the market served, including how inventory distribution affects equipment availability; how equipment shortages or other disruptions may affect bookings and mitigation strategies in place to anticipate and address such issues; how the common carrier’s policies and practices for determining and maintaining an adequate supply of containers/equipment based on cargo volume, type, and transport costs in the markets served. “Blank sailings” – The common carrier’s definition of blank sailings, policy and practices for cancelling sailings, including the timing and all communication mechanisms for notifying shippers of such blankings, and mitigation strategies to assist with export cargo bookings affected by blankings; how the cascading effects across schedules and operations are addressed. “Sweeper vessels” – A detailed explanation of the common carrier’s rules, practices, policies and/or performance targets concerning the designation, and the use, of sweeper vessels. Under the regulation, a sweeper vessel “means a vessel exclusively designated to load and move empty containers from a U.S. port for the purpose of transporting them to another designated location.” “Alternative remedies or assistance” – A detailed explanation of the common carrier’s rules, practices, policies and/or performance targets for providing alternative vessel space accommodations to an export shipper denied space, including the circumstances under which each alternative is considered or offered. A detailed explanation of how affected export shippers can request assistance and where such resources are found on the carrier’s website. 5. If any topics listed under 541.2(j)(1)(i), 541.2(j)(1)(ii), and/or 541.2(j)(1)(iii) are not addressed in a documented export policy because they are not applicable, the documented export policy should attest to this inapplicability clearly and unambiguously and provide a detailed factual explanation for non-applicability. 6. Submissions must be signed by a duly authorized officer of the regulated party with a copy of evidence of the officer’s authority. Each documented export policy must clearly identify the common carrier’s: FMC organization number, legal name, and all associated trade name(s) if applicable. This ensures that documented export policies are properly accredited to the correct organization and that a common carrier is not deemed to be in violation of the regulation. A documented export policy of a parent company may cover subsidiary companies in addition to the parent company. However, the documented export policy must clearly identify for the parent company and each subsidiary covered: the FMC organization number, the legal name of the company, and all associated trade name(s), if applicable. Unless such information is clearly identified, the FMC will consider the submission as applicable only to the parent company. Documented export policies will not be circulated outside of the Federal Maritime Commission. These documents, and the information contained therein, are not publicly disclosable, in whole or in part, including in response to requests under the Freedom of Information Act. Failure to file a documented export policy by March 1 constitutes a violation of a federal regulation. A person that violates a regulation or order of the Commission is liable to the United States Government for a civil penalty. 46 U.S.C. 41107(a). “Each day of a continuing violation is a separate violation,” with a current maximum penalty of $14,988 per violation, or $74,943 where the violation was willful and knowing. Id.; 46 CFR 506.4(d). Additionally, submission of knowingly fraudulent statements or misrepresentation in response to this requirement, or any other regulation or agency order, can result in criminal prosecution under 18 U.S.C. 1001, which, upon conviction, carries criminal penalties of a fine, up to five years of imprisonment, or both.

articles.title: Floating Production Outlook: Pipeline Looks Huge, But Not All Projects Are Created Equal
articles.summary: Global floating hydrocarbons and electricity production and storage infrastructure (floating units) has a sizeable development pipeline through 2035, but the gap between identified projects and committed work is substantial. Intelatus Global Partners tracks 711 floating units worldwide…
articles.body: Floating Production Outlook: Pipeline Looks Huge, But Not All Projects Are Created Equal Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. Alisa Reiner , Contributor Alisa Reiner is an independent contributor. Alisa brings experience in both... November 18, 2026 Figure 1. World map of selected installed and future pipeline floating units. Map note: The map covers 327 geographically assigned FPSO and FLNG units across all recorded years. Five Available units have no first-production year or geographic deployment and are excluded. Only countries with recorded FPSO/FLNG projects are shaded; darker red indicates larger regional totals. GOM = Gulf of Mexico, LATAM = Latin America, APAC = Asia-Pacific. Source: Intelatus Global Partners. Figure 2. Regional floating infrastructure composition by type, all recorded years. Source: Intelatus Global Partners. Figure 3. Floating units by region and status, all recorded years. Note: Five “Available” units have no geographic affiliation and are excluded from regional totals; Figures 1 and 2 therefore cover 706 units. Source: Floating Units Database, Intelatus Global Partners (October 2026); calculations by author. Figure 4. Planned and on-order floating units by expected first-production year, 2026–2035. Source: Intelatus Global Partners. Global floating hydrocarbons and electricity production and storage infrastructure (floating units) has a sizeable development pipeline through 2035, but the gap between identified projects and committed work is substantial. Intelatus Global Partners tracks 711 floating units worldwide, including 232 planned or on-order facilities with expected first-production dates in 2026–2035 . The commercial implications extend beyond floating unit construction. A deepwater FPSO in LATAM, a SEMI in the Gulf of Mexico, and an FSRU at a coastal terminal involve different mooring systems, installation sequences, and vessel requirements. For mooring suppliers and offshore support vessel owners, project maturity, water depth, and regional charter conditions will determine how much of the identified pipeline becomes executable work. A Large Fleet, but Not a Single Market Analysis covers 460 installed, 72 on order, 174 planned, and five available units. APAC leads the installed fleet with 137 units, followed by LATAM (93) and Africa (89). FPSOs account for 181 installed units, ahead of FSOs (74), FSRUs (48), and SEMIs (40) . APAC, LATAM, and Africa together account for 492 of the 711 recorded units, but their status mix distinguishes operating assets from prospective work (Figure 1). 174 planned units outnumber the 72 on order by more than two to one, and the main uncertainty is how much of that prospective work becomes contracted installations. Where the Units Are LATAM has 99 FPSOs among 145 units, whereas the Gulf of Mexico has 25 SEMIs and only ten FPSOs. The Mediterranean Sea is dominated by FSRUs (20 of 34 units), a different installation market from offshore production. \APAC has the largest regional fleet (217 units), spread across 74 FPSOs, 50 FSOs, 25 FSRUs, and other designs. Its 68 projects dated 2026–2035 span production, storage, and LNG import rather than one offshore installation profile. As for water depths, regional means are 1,564 m in LATAM, 1,402.3 m in the Gulf of Mexico, 889 m in Africa, 509 m in the Mediterranean Sea, 328 m in APAC, and 297 m in North Europe . However, APAC’s lower average masks considerable variation — Indonesia and India are emerging as markets for ultra-deepwater drilling. Yet a simple geographical unit count is an incomplete measure of supplier demand. Commercial interest is forward-looking. LATAM has 52 planned or on-order units dated 2026–2035, including 41 FPSOs; Brazil accounts for 30 projects and Guyana for 11. Its 21 units in 2031–2035 give it the largest regional pipeline for that later period. Africa has 41 planned or on-order units scheduled for 2026–2035, including 23 FPSOs and seven FLNG facilities. Nigeria accounts for 14 projects, while Namibia has six. All 13 African units dated 2031–2035 remain planned, so their conversion into installation work still depends on project sanction and procurement. The Gulf of Mexico features 21 planned or on-order units dated 2026–2035, including nine SEMIs, versus four FPSOs and four FLNG facilities. Its prospective installation mix therefore differs materially from FPSO-led LATAM. FPSOs Drive the Production Pipeline Of the 232 planned or on-order facilities dated 2026–2035, 108 are FPSOs (47%), compared with 30 FLNG units, 33 FSRUs, 15 SEMIs, and 17 FSOs (Table 1). The remaining 29 units are other floating infrastructure types. Unit type 2026–2030 2031–2035 Total FPSO 70 38 108 FLNG 16 14 30 SEMIs 8 7 15 FSRUs 29 4 33 FSOs 17 0 17 Other floating units 24 5 29 Total 164 68 232 Source: Intelatus Global Partners. Notably, interest in FLNG is broadening. Yinson Production , an established FPSO operator, is looking to extend its lease-and-operate model to FLNG, applying its experience in development, construction, and operations to offshore gas projects. In Brazil, Petrobras has sought market information on potential FLNG options for its offshore gas resources. Rystad Energy expects global FLNG capacity to rise from 14.1 Mtpa in 2024 to 42 Mtpa by 2030 and 55 Mtpa by 2035, supported by stronger operating performance and the economics of smaller or remote gas fields. The IEA projects more than 330 bcm/year of new LNG export capacity entering service over 2025–2030. This includes onshore plants as well as floating facilities, but the sheer scope is illustrative. T he Schedule Gets Less Certain After 2030 Expected first production peaks in 2028 at 52 units, evenly split between 26 on order and 26 planned (Figure 3). This is not the offshore installation peak: mooring pre-lay and floater hook-up normally occur before first production, and project delays could shift that workload across years. Project maturity is a greater uncertainty than the precise annual profile. Of the 164 units dated 2026–2030, 70 are on order and 94 are planned. In 2031–2035, just two are on order and 66 remain planned. Schedules can move, and some developments may never reach sanction. Conversely, newly added projects could increase demand after 2030. Importantly, the installed fleet is not a static base to which all pipeline projects can simply be added. Some units will retire; others will remain on their fields longer, be modified, or be redeployed. The database does not contain a complete schedule of retirements and redeployments, so the identified pipeline is not a forecast of net fleet growth. Similarly, redeployment does not necessarily require building a new hull, but it could involve repair, new moorings, underwater operations, and reinstatement. Mooring Design Determines Installation Scope Floater architecture and field conditions determine the mooring scope. A turret-moored FPSO, spread-moored SEMI, and tension-leg platform transmit station-keeping loads differently and require different installation sequences. Water depth, metocean loading, and seabed conditions affect mooring geometry, line length, strength, materials, and anchor choice, including whether drag-embedment, suction, or torpedo anchors are suitable. These choices set vessel and handling requirements. A typical deepwater chain–polyester–chain system can involve separate campaigns for anchor installation, line pre-lay, and floater hook-up. Installation loads and methods, rather than floater type alone, determine anchor handling tug supply (AHTS) vessels’ bollard pull, winch and deck capacity, and the number of loadouts required. A single development can therefore generate work across floating facilities, moorings, and subsea systems. For suppliers, this makes a combined assessment of floater type and regional conditions essential — it is their interaction that determines the technical specifications of mooring systems, installation requirements, and ultimately the type and capacity of offshore support vessels (OSV) needed. Charter Markets Shape OSV Availability Market factors also matter. Charter terms can restrict the pool of suitable vessels for other projects. For instance, in Brazil, DOF secured four-year awards for four AHTS vessels, including one with more than 350 tons of bollard pull and three configured for deepwater remotely operated vehicle (ROV) vessel work. Such long-term commitments secure utilization for owners while limiting high-specification vessel availability elsewhere. North Sea vessel tightness in 2025-2026 has been partly linked to longer Brazilian commitments. Conversely, West Africa is more short-term campaign-driven: vessels often get mobilized there from the North Sea, moving south during the northern hemisphere winter. Summer returns are possible, not automatic; mobilization costs, contract terms, local requirements, and weather windows govern the economics. The Commercial Outlook The key message is that the floating market should be read as a portfolio of very different offshore campaigns rather than a single global trend. LATAM remains the deepest pool of FPSO demand, but it is also one of the markets where large, long-duration projects can tie up high-specification tonnage and absorb substantial mooring scope. APAC is broader and less uniform: it combines production, storage, and gas infrastructure, while parts of the region are now moving further into deepwater. Africa offers both established FPSO work and a growing gas-related story, but much of the later pipeline still has to convert from planning into funded execution. For suppliers, that means market entry should be based on technical fit and regional positioning, not just on the headline number of units. The more forward-looking point is that project quality now matters more than project count. The 2026–2030 pipeline contains the bulk of identified near-term work, but after 2030 the market becomes more gas-heavy and much less certain, with most units still only planned. That creates a premium for companies that can screen pipelines early, follow the shift from concept to commitment, and match vessels, moorings, and installation methods to the projects most likely to move. In practice, the winners are likely to be those positioned where three conditions overlap: a credible project backlog, technical complexity that limits competition, and local market access. That is where floating-unit activity turns into real commercial demand. Photo Credit Shlomo Shoham Israeli containership operator ZIM Integrated Shipping Services reported a sharp increase in third-quarter 2026 earnings, driven by stronger freight rates, higher cargo volumes and improved operating margins, prompting the company to raise its full-year financial guidance. ZIM reported third-quarter revenue of $2.71 billion, up 53% from $1.78 billion a year earlier. Net income surged to $830 million from $123 million, while adjusted EBITDA more than doubled to $1.33 billion. The company carried 962,000 TEUs during the quarter, a 4% year-over-year increase, while average freight rates climbed 55% to $2,480 per TEU from $1,602. Adjusted EBIT reached $993 million, representing a 37% margin, compared with 15% in the corresponding 2025 period. “By keeping our network agile and focusing on premium, profitable trades, we are supporting our customers and positioning ZIM for further growth,” said Chen Lichtenstein, ZIM President and CEO. ZIM also generated $1.22 billion in quarterly free cash flow, strengthening its balance sheet and reducing net debt to $1.86 billion. Fleet Development and Orderbook ZIM currently operates 112 containerships with aggregate capacity of approximately 703,000 TEUs, alongside 13 car carriers. During the second half of 2026, the company took delivery of two newly built 8,000-TEU containerships under five-to-seven-year charters. Its charter orderbook includes 56 vessels, comprising 52 containerships totaling approximately 418,000 TEUs and four car carriers. The newbuilding program includes 18 LNG dual-fuel containerships of 11,500 TEUs each. ZIM also expanded its service network, launching the ZX3 expedited Asia–U.S. West Coast service and Falcon service connecting China with Argentina and southern Brazil. Reflecting stronger market conditions, ZIM raised its 2026 adjusted EBITDA forecast to $3.3 billion–$3.5 billion, from $2.7 billion–$3 billion previously. Meanwhile, Hapag-Lloyd's proposed $35-per-share acquisition of ZIM remains subject to regulatory approvals, including Israeli government consent. The transaction is targeted for completion in the first quarter of 2027. ZIM declared a dividend of $2.01 per share, totaling approximately $243 million.

articles.title: NYK Names Gas Carrier with Ammonia-Fueled Engines Izanami
articles.summary: Japan's NYK has named Izanami, a newly built 40,000-cu.m. medium gas carrier equipped with ammonia-fueled main and auxiliary engines, marking a milestone in the development of ammonia propulsion for commercial shipping.Built at Japan Marine…
articles.body: NYK Names Gas Carrier with Ammonia-Fueled Engines Izanami Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 18, 2026 Image courtesy NYK Japan's NYK has named Izanami, a newly built 40,000-cu.m. medium gas carrier equipped with ammonia-fueled main and auxiliary engines, marking a milestone in the development of ammonia propulsion for commercial shipping. Built at Japan Marine United Corporation's Ariake Shipyard in Kumamoto Prefecture, the vessel was named November 6 by NYK President Takaya Soga , followed by an unveiling ceremony November 17. According to NYK, Izanami is the world's first vessel equipped with ammonia-fueled engines for both propulsion and onboard power generation. The ship features a dual-fuel, two-stroke main engine manufactured by Japan Engine Corporation and dual-fuel, four-stroke auxiliary engines supplied by IHI Power Systems. The 180-meter vessel has a breadth of 32 meters and molded depth of 18.45 meters and will operate under the Japanese flag. The project is part of Japan's New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO) Green Innovation Fund , established to accelerate the development and commercialization of technologies supporting carbon neutrality by 2050. NYK, Japan Engine Corporation, IHI Power Systems and Nihon Shipyard were selected for the program in October 2021. Working with classification society ClassNK , the partners have developed domestically produced ammonia propulsion technology for commercial vessels. Following delivery, Izanami will be time-chartered to Yara Clean Ammonia Switzerland SA , part of Norway's Yara International . The charter will include demonstration voyages to evaluate engine performance, operational safety and greenhouse gas reductions under actual operating conditions. Although ammonia combustion produces no carbon dioxide, its use as marine fuel presents technical challenges involving toxicity, fuel handling and emissions management. The operational trials will provide data to support future ammonia-fueled vessel development. The project builds on NYK's experience with Sakigake, an ammonia-fueled tugboat that entered commercial service in August 2024, also developed under the NEDO program. With Izanami moving into operation, NYK and its partners will transition from engine and vessel development to collecting performance data from commercial voyages, supporting efforts to establish ammonia as a viable alternative marine fuel for deep-sea shipping.
