articles.title: Shipping Organizations Urges IMO Agreement on GHG Regulations
articles.summary: Nine major international shipping associations have issued a joint appeal to governments to reach agreement on global greenhouse gas (GHG) regulations, warning that continued regulatory uncertainty could undermine investment in alternative fuels…
articles.body: Shipping Organizations Urges IMO Agreement on GHG Regulations Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 18, 2026 Nine major international shipping associations have issued a joint appeal to governments to reach agreement on global greenhouse gas (GHG) regulations, warning that continued regulatory uncertainty could undermine investment in alternative fuels, fleet renewal and maritime decarbonization. The statement comes ahead of the International Maritime Organization's Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85), scheduled to meet in London from November 30 to December 4, 2026. The organizations—BIMCO, CLIA, IBIA, ICS, INTERCARGO, INTERFERRY, INTERTANKO, IPTA and the World Shipping Council—represent the global commercial shipping fleet across virtually every major maritime sector. While reaffirming support for the IMO's 2023 GHG Strategy, which targets net-zero emissions by or around 2050, the associations emphasized that future regulations must be practical, enforceable and economically achievable. Central to their position is the need for a single global framework that applies equally to ships regardless of flag, ownership or trade. The organizations cautioned against fragmented regional or national regulations that could impose duplicate compliance requirements or multiple charges on the same emissions. The statement also calls for regulations that reward verified emissions reductions, incentivize investment in commercially viable alternative fuels and provide flexible compliance mechanisms for shipowners. The associations acknowledged that zero and near-zero GHG fuels and technologies remain commercially unavailable for much of the existing global fleet, making realistic transition pathways essential. Shipowners have already invested billions of dollars in alternative-fuel-capable vessels and emerging technologies, but further investment depends on regulatory certainty and the availability of competitively priced alternative fuels at scale. The organizations urged IMO member states to engage constructively with competing proposals and develop a technology-neutral framework supported by clear technical guidance, including fuel certification and lifecycle emissions assessment. They stressed that an agreement is needed as soon as practicable to provide the investment confidence necessary for shipping's energy transition.

articles.body: Collaboration November 18, 2026 · 4 minutes ago Orlen spreads its wings across Central and Eastern Europe with new gas pacts U.S. LNG is expected to reach more European energy markets as Orlen’s new partnerships strengthen regional cooperation. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email LNG carrier Source: Orlen Orlen, a Polish multi-sector company, is expanding its gas business across Central and Eastern European Countries (CEECs) through new agreements and partnerships with energy companies in Ukraine, Slovakia and Hungary, highlighting Poland’s growing role as a regional gateway for global gas supplies and the firm’s ambitions to strengthen energy security while expanding its commercial footprint across the region. Orlen has revealed that it will supply Ukraine with natural gas from three LNG cargoes under a new contract with Naftogaz. This gas will originate from the United States and, following regasification at the LNG terminal in Świnoujście, will be transported via gas pipelines to Ukraine. The agreement, which will ensure the continuity of gas supplies to the Ukrainian market in the first quarter of 2027, is of significant importance in strengthening the energy security of the region, according to the Polish player. " Thanks to our continuously developing commercial expertise, our own LNG transport vessels and access to regasification capacity, we can effectively support Ukraine in diversifying its sources and routes of natural gas supply. This is particularly important in the face of growing threats to Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Our activities strengthen the region’s energy security whilst delivering tangible business benefits. " — Robert Soszyński Vice President of the Orlen Management Board for Operations Orlen has been developing its commercial partnership with Naftogaz since 2025. During this time, the companies have concluded five contracts for the supply of over 600 million cubic meters of gas derived from the regasification of U.S. LNG imported to the terminals in Świnoujście and Klaipėda. " Our strategic partnership with Orlen allows us to secure US LNG supplies in the first quarter of 2027 and provide additional resilience during peak periods of winter gas demand. Amid ongoing Russian attacks, alongside our efforts to protect and restore our facilities, we are working to secure reliable sources and routes of gas supply. " — Sergii Fedorenko Acting Chief Executive Officer of Naftogaz Related Articles Clean Fuel Orlen and Naftogaz deepen energy ties with two MoUs 2 min read Orlen and Slovakia’s Slovenský plynárenský priemysel (SPP) have also signed an agreement revolving around a wider choice of gas sources for Slovakia and new sales opportunities for the Polish player, opening a new phase of talks on gas supplies using LNG imported into Poland. " We want to turn our experience in LNG sourcing and gas trading into new sales opportunities in Central and Eastern Europe. The agreement with SPP, Slovakia’s largest energy supplier, opens up the prospect of working with a partner of key importance to this market. Our goal is clear: to grow Orlen’s business and develop a competitive offering that gives our partners greater flexibility in purchasing gas. In this way, we combine our commercial ambitions with the region’s energy security. " — Ireneusz Fąfara President of the Management Board of Orlen The cooperation is based on LNG, which, once delivered to a terminal in Poland and regasified, could reach SPP through European gas networks. The talks will cover gas sources, commercial terms, and delivery arrangements. The partnership gives the duo flexibility to tailor their offering to market needs. The agreement also aligns with the objectives of REPowerEU, representing the EU’s plan to end dependence on Russian fossil fuels through energy savings, the development of renewable energy sources, and supply diversification, requiring a need to build commercial relationships with alternative suppliers and expand access to gas from a variety of sources. " SPP is intensively preparing for the period beyond 2027, when imports of Russian natural gas into the European Union will be phased out in accordance with REPowerEU legislation. Our priority is to ensure reliable and competitively priced natural gas supplies for our customers under these new conditions. Poland and Orlen represent a promising opportunity to further diversify our supply portfolio. The use of LNG terminals in Poland could provide Slovakia with access to additional natural gas sources on the global market while expanding the options for transporting gas to our country. " — Martin Húska Chief Executive Officer and Member of the Board of Directors of SPP Related Articles Clean Fuel EU endorses ban on Russian pipeline gas and LNG imports 3 min read Meanwhile, Orlen and Hungary’s MVM ONEnergy have signed a memorandum on potential cooperation in LNG deliveries to Polish terminals, regasification, and the transportation of natural gas to Hungary to assess solutions that support the security and diversification of gas supplies. Advertisement " Energy security in Central and Eastern Europe requires diverse gas supply sources and transportation routes, as well as cooperation between partners across the region. In our discussions with MVM ONEnergy, we want to draw on Orlen’s experience in LNG sourcing and organizing gas deliveries to European markets. The memorandum with MVM ONEnergy brings together two important objectives for us: strengthening the region’s energy security and expanding Orlen’s presence in the Hungarian market. " — Fąfara underlined. This cooperation aligns with the development of the Baltic Eagle Gas Hub concept, a regional center for gas supply and trading, combining access to the global LNG market with Baltic import infrastructure and cross-border interconnections. An important element of this concept is leveraging the potential of U.S. LNG supplies and strengthening Poland’s role as a gateway for U.S. gas to Central and Eastern Europe. The concept is supported by the capacity used and reserved at the Świnoujście and Klaipėda terminals and the planned FSRU terminals in the Gulf of Gdańsk, complemented by Orlen’s own fleet of LNG carriers. Expanding cooperation with customers in Central and Eastern Europe is intended to turn this potential into increased sales for the Polish firm while broadening the choice of gas sources and strengthening security of supply across the region. articles.body: Europe Offshore Neo Next+ snaps up EnQuest’s North Sea business in $960m deal Bojan Lepic November 18, 2026 0 282 1 minute read EnQuest EnQuest UK offshore producer Neo Next+ Energy has agreed to acquire EnQuest’s entire UK upstream oil and gas business in a deal worth up to $960m, further consolidating its position as the largest producer on the UK Continental Shelf. The transaction involves acquiring EnQuest Britain Limited for $840m in upfront cash, with a further $120m potentially payable depending on oil prices and changes to the UK’s Energy Profits Levy. The portfolio includes producing interests in the operated Kraken, Magnus, and Greater Kittiwake Area fields, alongside a non-operated stake in Golden Eagle. The deal also covers the undeveloped Bressay and Bentley discoveries and infrastructure including the Sullom Voe Terminal, Northern Leg Gas Pipeline, and Ninian Pipeline system. The assets produced approximately 31,100 barrels of oil equivalent per day in 2025, with 92% coming from liquids. At the end of last year, the portfolio held 122m barrels of oil equivalent in proven and probable reserves and 308m barrels in contingent resources. Neo Next+ executive chair John Knight said the acquisition would strengthen the company’s scale, production base and cash flow while supporting further consolidation of the UK offshore industry. The deal follows a series of major transactions by the company, which completed its merger with Repsol’s UK upstream business in July 2025 before combining with TotalEnergies’ British offshore operations in March 2026. Meanwhile, the disposal marks a major strategic shift for EnQuest, which is increasingly concentrating on Southeast Asia. In June, the company announced acquisitions worth up to $833m covering interests in four production sharing contracts offshore Malaysia. After completing those transactions and the UK disposal, EnQuest expects its Southeast Asian operations to produce around 70,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, based on 2025 figures. EnQuest will retain its Veri Energy business and associated carbon capture interests. The North Sea transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and completion of EnQuest’s Malaysian acquisitions. articles.body: Containers Europe Offen firms up four-ship boxship comeback in China Adis Ajdin November 18, 2026 0 683 1 minute read GSI GSI German tonnage provider Claus-Peter Offen has reportedly firmed up all four of its planned 7,000 teu containership newbuildings, ending a nearly two-decade absence from the ordering market. Shipbuilding sources say the Hamburg-based owner has committed to the full quartet after initially signing a letter of intent in September for two firm vessels and two options. China’s Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI), part of state-owned CSSC, remains linked to the deal, although the builder has yet to be formally confirmed. No contract price or firm delivery dates have emerged, with earlier market reports pointing to slots around 2030. The conventionally powered ships would add around 28,000 teu to Offen’s fleet and mark its first containership orders since 2007. Market sources have also suggested that the four vessels have secured charter backing from one of the world’s ten largest liner operators. The charterer’s identity and employment terms have not been disclosed. The newbuildings fall into a segment where Chinese yards have attracted growing interest from both liner operators and tonnage providers. One of the designs gaining traction is SDARI’s compact Sealion 7100, which measures 255 m in length and 42.8 m in breadth, with capacity for up to 1,143 reefer containers. The final specification of Offen’s ships has not been confirmed. For comparison, South Korea’s Namsung Shipping has recently been linked to two firm 7,100 teu ships plus two options at China’s Dalian Shipbuilding Industry Corporation, with brokers putting the price at around $89m per vessel. Offen’s return to ordering follows years of relying on older tonnage, much of it employed by major liners including MSC and Ocean Network Express. Its last containership newbuilding programme dates back to before the 2008 financial crisis, with the final vessels arriving several years later after construction delays. Among the youngest ships stemming from that earlier investment are the 2012-built, 5,574 teu MSC Coruna and MSC Vigo, both still listed in the company’s fleet under MSC employment. Founded in 1971, Offen remains one of Germany’s largest non-operating containership owners, with its website listing more than 40 vessels under management. articles.body: Interconnectors November 18, 2026 · 1 minute ago Greece: Dodecanese islands' link to mainland awarded €228.9 million EU grant NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Source: CINEA An interconnector that will link Greece's Dodecanese islands to the mainland electricity grid has secured the largest grant ever awarded under the European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency's (CINEA) European Public Sector Loan Facility program, amounting to €228.9 million. The interconnection will be delivered in two phases, with the first to include a high-voltage direct current (HVDC) submarine link between the mainland point in Corinth and the island of Kos, together with two AC/DC converter stations and the associated transmission infrastructure. With an estimated budget of €2.54 billion, phase 1 is supported under the Public Sector Loan Facility (PSLF) through a €228.9 million EU grant combined with a €1.53 billion loan from the European Investment Bank (EIB), representing the largest contribution to a single project under the PSLF to date. The first project phase also benefits from a €534 million grant from the Greek Decarbonisation Fund. “The Dodecanese interconnection project is an excellent example of how Greece, the European Commission and the European Investment Bank can work together to turn clean energy ambitions into reality,” said European Commission Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy Director Emma Toledano . “It will make a real difference to island communities, bringing them a cheaper and more reliable electricity supply while making it easier to use more renewable energy from a larger and more flexible grid. In doing so, the project shows what a socially just energy transition can look like in practice.” Related Articles Interconnectors Nexans to deliver 420 kilometers of cable for Greek interconnection 1 min read According to CINEA, Phase 1 alone is expected to cut CO2 emissions by around 7.7 million tons over 25 years, roughly 309,000 tons per year. By connecting the islands to the mainland grid, the project will also open the way for more renewable energy in the region, contributing directly to the energy and climate objectives of both the EU and Greece. The project's second phase, which is not part of the EU-supported project, will add AC interconnections to bring Rhodes and Karpathos into the system. Once completed, the two phases will end the Dodecanese islands’ electrical isolation, relieve grid saturation and allow polluting oil-fired power plants to be decommissioned. “The Dodecanese electricity interconnection project, currently being implemented by IPTO, will permanently end the region’s energy isolation, accelerate the phase-out of polluting oil-fired power plants, and unlock the renewable energy potential of the Aegean Sea," said Manos Manousakis , Chairman and CEO of the Greek transmission system operator (TSO), Independent Power Transmission Operator (IPTO). "The investment not only strengthens security of supply, but also lowers consumer costs, drives sustainable economic growth, and ensures a more resilient, interconnected grid across every corner of Greece. Securing the largest grant awarded to date under this EU funding program – alongside crucial backing from EIB and the Greek Decarbonisation Fund - marks a major milestone in our country’s energy transition." articles.title: Shipping heavyweights warn against double carbon charges
articles.summary: Nine of the world’s leading shipping associations have joined forces to push governments towards a global emissions deal, warning that a patchwork of regional regulations risks leaving shipowners paying multiple times for the same carbon emissions. The joint intervention comes ahead of a crucial round of talks at the...
articles.body: Environment Operations Regulatory Shipping heavyweights warn against double carbon charges Adis Ajdin November 18, 2026 0 337 2 minutes read IMO IMO Nine of the world’s leading shipping associations have joined forces to push governments towards a global emissions deal, warning that a patchwork of regional regulations risks leaving shipowners paying multiple times for the same carbon emissions. The joint intervention comes ahead of a crucial round of talks at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) later this month, with governments still divided over how to regulate and price shipping’s greenhouse gas emissions. BIMCO, the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), Intercargo, Intertanko, the World Shipping Council, Cruise Lines International Association (CLIA), Interferry, the International Bunker Industry Association (IBIA) and the International Parcel Tankers Association (IPTA) have called for a single global framework that applies equally to vessels regardless of flag, ownership or trade. “Shipping is a global industry requiring global rules applied equally to all ships,” the organisations said. The groups warned that national and regional schemes could result in duplicated compliance requirements and multiple charges for the same emissions, undermining efforts to establish a level playing field. They want an IMO agreement that rewards verifiable emissions reductions while giving shipowners sufficient flexibility to manage the transition to cleaner fuels, many of which remain commercially unavailable for much of the existing fleet. The joint statement also calls for regulations that are fuel- and technology-neutral, enforceable and backed by clear incentives for investment in alternative fuels and energy-saving technologies. The intervention comes after the IMO failed to secure agreement on its proposed Net-Zero Framework in October 2025, forcing governments to postpone adoption for a year. The framework, which combines a global marine fuel standard with an emissions-pricing mechanism, remains the subject of negotiations over its cost, design and implementation. The industry’s latest appeal follows growing concern over the spread of regional carbon schemes. Several African governments are moving towards their own shipping emissions charges, while European operators already face the EU Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime regulations. The nine associations warned that the lack of regulatory certainty is complicating investment decisions for shipowners, ports, fuel producers and financiers, particularly given the limited availability and high cost of lower-emissions fuels. Governments will resume negotiations at the IMO’s greenhouse gas working group from November 23 to 27, followed by the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s 85th session from November 30 to December 3. A further extraordinary session to consider adoption of the emissions framework could take place on December 4, subject to confirmation during MEPC 85. articles.body: Bunkering Environment Europe Operations Regulatory UK sets out 2030 marine fuel crackdown Adis Ajdin November 18, 2026 0 434 1 minute read UK Government UK Government Britain has laid out plans for a new shipping fuel regulation that could initially cover around 5,000 vessels calling at its ports, including ships operating on international routes. The Department for Transport opened a consultation this week on a proposed greenhouse gas intensity standard, which the government expects to introduce from 2030. The regime would initially apply to ships of 5,000 gt and above, irrespective of flag, requiring operators to progressively reduce the lifecycle emissions intensity of the fuels and energy they use. Under the government’s preferred approach, the rules would cover all energy consumed on domestic voyages, half the energy used on voyages between British and foreign ports, and emissions generated while ships are alongside in the UK. The obligation would fall on shipping companies rather than bunker suppliers. Britain is taking its lead from the EU’s FuelEU Maritime framework, which entered into force in January 2025, while seeking to retain flexibility around future IMO requirements. Government modelling suggests 4,913 vessels of at least 5,000 gt called at UK ports in 2019. Another 2,405 smaller ships could eventually be brought into the regime if the threshold is lowered to 400 gt. The consultation leaves several important questions unresolved, including how quickly emissions limits should tighten, how operators could pool or trade compliance credits, and the penalties for missing targets. The latest move comes after domestic shipping was brought into the UK Emissions Trading Scheme in July. British shipowners have already warned against copying the administrative problems encountered under FuelEU Maritime. In October, the UK Chamber of Shipping called for better-aligned reporting systems and realistic targets reflecting the availability of alternative fuels. The consultation closes on February 22, 2027. articles.summary: The U.S. Coast Guard's largest icebreaker, USCGC Healy, suffered a catastrophic overspeed failure of one of its main propulsion diesel generators in July, triggering a fire in the generator room and requiring extensive repairs to electrical and fire-detection systems, and corrective maintenance affecting two...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network The Coast Guard Cutter Healy (WAGB-20), a polar-class icebreaker, transits Southeast Alaskan waters Nov. 24, 2018. U.S. Coast Guard Photo Procurement records now establish that the incident involved more than an isolated engine casualty, with a subsequent fire and extensive damage to equipment in Generator Room No. 2, alongside corrective maintenance requirements affecting two additional generators. The U.S. Coast Guard’s largest icebreaker, USCGC Healy , suffered a catastrophic overspeed failure of one of its main propulsion diesel generators in July, triggering a fire in the generator room and requiring extensive repairs to electrical and fire-detection systems, and corrective maintenance affecting two additional engines, according to Coast Guard procurement documents. The documents provide the most detailed account yet of the incident aboard the 420-foot icebreaker, which was towed back to its homeport in Seattle on July 13 after experiencing a significant engineering casualty while operating northwest of Port Angeles, Washington . The Coast Guard announced the incident on July 24, saying Healy would undergo major repairs and an investigation. The vessel subsequently abandoned its planned 2026 high-latitude summer mission . The decision to end icebreaker Healy ’s planned high-latitude mission left the service leaning more heavily on its newest icebreaker during an increasingly active Arctic season . A procurement document issued in October for corrective maintenance on two of Healy ‘s other main propulsion diesel generators provides a more specific description of the incident, stating: “CGC HEALY suffered a catastrophic overspeed failure of its #2 MPDG.” The document also recommended immediate corrective action on the overspeed protection devices and governor equipment on generators No. 1 and No. 3. A separate September procurement document for an overhaul of Healy ‘s fire-detection system describes a subsequent fire in Generator Room No. 2 and the resulting damage. “The USCGC HEALY experienced an engine casualty in Generator Room #2 that resulted in a fire in the compartment,” the document states. “Fire detection equipment and wiring were exposed to high temperatures causing a ground fault in the system.” The document continues that “all equipment and wiring in the upper section of the Generator room will need to be renewed.” The fire also caused numerous faults in the detection system, while its Person Machine Interface (PMI-2) was experiencing problems retaining memory and required replacement. The Coast Guard sought a contractor to overhaul the Siemens FireFinder XLS system, including replacement of damaged detection equipment and wiring. The work was to be performed alongside at Coast Guard Base Seattle, with a completion deadline of October 16. The October solicitation provides further insight into the maintenance required following the failure of generator No. 2. The Coast Guard sought contractors to overhaul the mechanical and electro-pneumatic overspeed protection systems on generators No. 1 and No. 3, as well as their Woodward governors and associated equipment. The work included disassembly, inspection, cleaning, repair, recalibration and bench testing of the mechanical overspeed cutouts and electro-pneumatic limiters. The governors and their boosters were also to be removed, completely disassembled, inspected against original equipment manufacturer specifications, fitted with replacement seals and bearings, and bench tested. The solicitation contained another revealing detail about the condition of the machinery. “The governors and boosters appeared to be operating properly but there is no record of service or overhaul,” the document states. It adds that both engines had accumulated more than 40,000 operating hours. The work also included replacement of the A2 cylinder head on engine No. 3 because of damage to the dummy-valve seating surface and dummy-valve body. The removed cylinder head and valve were to be sent to a machine shop for inspection and reconditioning. The Coast Guard scheduled the corrective maintenance between October 13 and October 31 in Seattle. The contract also included an option for up to $60,000 in additional repairs if inspections identified further problems. Meanwhile, a separate procurement addressed the vessel’s CO2 fire-suppression system, including replacement of manual fire-pull equipment and associated cabling serving Generator Rooms No. 1 and No. 2. The documents do not establish whether all the contracted work has been completed or provide a revised return-to-service date for the icebreaker. Another procurement published November 13 provides a glimpse of the Coast Guard’s longer-term maintenance plans for Healy ‘s integrated propulsion plant. The Surface Forces Logistics Center is conducting market research for a five-year support requirement covering July 2028 through July 2033. The proposed contract would cover maintenance and technical support for the vessel’s integrated machinery plant and associated shoreside equipment. GE Power Conversion, part of GE Vernova, is identified as the original equipment manufacturer and holder of the proprietary data rights needed to provide the support. The previous contract was awarded to GE on a sole-source basis. The proposed scope includes periodic equipment maintenance, technical support and troubleshooting, casualty response, engineering analysis, configuration management, and replacement of obsolete components. It also specifically calls for hands-on and classroom training for both Healy ‘s permanent crew and Coast Guard shore-support personnel. The requirement includes evaluating equipment obsolescence and forecasting reliability, maintainability and availability concerns five years beyond the contract period. It also calls for technical upgrades intended to maintain operational availability through the vessel’s midlife maintenance period. The November notice is a sources-sought market survey rather than a request for proposals or an awarded contract. articles.summary: Oil is increasingly moving through the Strait of Hormuz on smaller vessels, helping sustain exports as attacks on supertankers squeeze availability of the ships that typically dominate the trade.

REUTERS/Amr Alfiky/File Photo By Weilun Soon Nov 18, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Oil is increasingly moving through the Strait of Hormuz on smaller vessels, helping sustain exports as attacks on supertankers squeeze availability of the ships that typically dominate the trade. The volume shipped through the waterway by Suezmaxes and Aframaxes has climbed over the past two months, hitting a wartime high of more than 2 million barrels a day in October, according to Vortexa. That helped elevate overall daily exports to 11.4 million barrels, the highest since the conflict began. The lucrative but risky trade of shuttling crude out of the Persian Gulf during the US-Iran war has primarily relied on very large crude carriers, which can carry up to 2 million barrels. The supertankers account for 72% of the vessels transiting Hormuz, according to BRS Shipbrokers, although they have become the target of Iranian attacks, taking some out of operation. The use of Suezmaxes and Aframaxes has helped ensure Gulf exports remain robust, according to shipbrokers and traders. The vessels, which carry less than half as much as a VLCC, have mostly been used to load cargoes from Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar, they said. The tankers either transfer crude to other ships after passing through Hormuz or sail directly to ports, often in India. The Lucia A is among the first Suezmaxes to enter the trade, ship-tracking data show. Since June, it’s picked up at least four cargoes from Iraq and delivered them to ships waiting in the Gulf of Oman or to Ain Sukhna, an Egyptian port in the Red Sea. Earlier this month, it loaded its fifth Iraqi shipment. Another Suezmax, the Ture, collected its third Iraqi cargo last week, according to ship-tracking data. The vessel previously transported crude from Russia’s western ports to India, a trade permitted as long as the oil complies with price-cap guidelines imposed by the Group of Seven nations. An attempt to contact the Marshall Islands-based owner of Lucia A was unsuccessful. The ship’s safety manager in Shanghai and the manager of Ture in Greece, did not immediately respond to emailed requests for comment. Smaller vessels also offer significantly lower freight costs. While they carry less crude, supertanker rates have risen much faster than those for other tankers since the start of the war. Shipbrokers have assessed the rate for a Suezmax traveling from the Persian Gulf to China at around a third to just under half the published benchmark rate for a VLCC on the same route. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. U.S. Coast Guard Photo The U.S. Coast Guard’s newest polar icebreaker, Storis (WAGB 21), has returned to Seattle following a 133-day Arctic deployment that included monitoring Chinese research vessels, conducting fisheries enforcement operations and testing military capabilities in ice-covered waters. The 360-foot cutter returned to its temporary homeport on Saturday, November 14, after traveling more than 17,000 nautical miles through the Arctic Ocean and waters around Alaska. According to the Coast Guard, Storis served as the sole U.S. surface asset in the High Arctic during portions of its deployment, supporting maritime security, border enforcement and sovereignty missions. Under Operation Frontier Sentinel, the cutter spent more than 300 hours monitoring foreign-flagged research vessels, including four Chinese-flagged ships operating over the U.S. extended continental shelf. The patrol also marked the first designated law enforcement mission conducted by a U.S. polar icebreaker in more than 20 years. The crew inspected fishing vessels in the Bering Sea, including a joint boarding and fisheries processing plant inspection with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Office of Law Enforcement. In another milestone, Storis conducted what the Coast Guard described as the first live-fire gunnery exercise by one of its surface vessels operating in ice-covered Arctic waters in decades. The exercise was intended to assess weapons employment in extreme conditions and generate data to guide future Arctic operations. The cutter also conducted a simulated replenishment-at-sea exercise with Coast Guard Cutter Stratton near Unalaska, Alaska. Crews used Storis’ dynamic positioning system and onboard sensors to demonstrate close-quarters maneuvering capabilities needed for replenishment operations in remote waters. During Operation Tundra Merlin, Storis operated alongside Coast Guard cutters Munro and Fir and the Royal Canadian Navy’s HMCS Max Bernays, strengthening coordination between U.S. and Canadian forces. The cutter also assisted the grounded fishing vessel Aleutian Dream, providing initial assistance and escorting the vessel back to Dutch Harbor. “We are serving in a moment of great change in our service, nation and world,” said Capt. Corey Kerns, commanding officer of Storis. He said the crew’s efforts had transformed the vessel into an operational, multi-mission military asset. The deployment included testing unmanned aircraft in extreme cold alongside the Coast Guard Research and Development Center and the Defense Innovation Unit. Five sorties totaling nine flight hours evaluated drone performance in high-latitude conditions, supporting the Icebreaker Collaboration Effort between the United States, Canada and Finland. Storis, formerly the commercial icebreaking vessel Aiviq, was acquired by the Coast Guard in December 2024 and commissioned in August 2025, becoming the service’s first new polar icebreaker in more than two decades. The deployment comes as the Coast Guard’s already limited polar icebreaking fleet faces continued strain. The service’s medium icebreaker Healy has been sidelined since suffering a major engineering casualty in July, forcing the cancellation of its planned 2026 Arctic mission. The situation underscores Washington’s continuing struggle to maintain polar capabilities as competition with Russia and China intensifies.
